questions.explanation: The logistic form is built on three idealisations, and each of them is known to fail in a real series. It writes one rate of increase for the whole population, so age structure, size structure and any genetic or physiological variation in reproductive rate are averaged away, and a population dominated by a few fertile individuals is badly mis-described by it. It puts the crowding effect on the current population size alone, with no term for the time it takes offspring to become reproductive, which is the delay that produces overshoot. And it treats the carrying capacity as a property of the site, although it moves with the season, with the weather and with anything else that changes the supply. None of these is a reason to discard the model, since it is still the best single-curve summary available, and each is a reason to check the residuals rather than the fit.

answer.ex: The outcome that matters is the disease, not the insect count, so the design has to be powered on cases and has to run long enough to cover at least one transmission season and ideally two, since a single season is easily dominated by weather. The comparison should be a cluster trial rather than an individual one, because a household taking part in the programme stops being a naive case in the neighbourhood, so the unit of randomisation is the village or the block, with a matched untreated set of comparable villages that receive the programme afterwards. Baseline data have to be collected before the programme starts, because the two groups will differ in ways that are not related to the intervention and a single end-of-programme comparison cannot remove them; the analysis is a difference in differences on the case rate per population, which also controls for a district-wide change in reporting or in access to treatment. Two outcomes are needed rather than one. The case rate answers the question that matters, and the larval or adult density answers whether the programme did what it was supposed to do, because a fall in cases with no fall in the vector density would mean something other than the water removal is operating and the programme would be about to fail. Counts must be taken over comparable effort, using the same sampling frame and the same catching method in both arms, and the source of the cases should be confirmed in a fixed fraction so that a change in diagnosis does not masquerade as a change in disease. Finally the programme has to be checked for the two ways this kind of intervention usually fails: households that empty the water once and then return to the habit, which shows up as a recovery in the density measures, and displacement, where the mosquitoes move to the next village, which is why the untreated comparison villages have to be surrounded by treated ones rather than being scattered through the treated area.
